## Summary

Research confidence is **Moderate**. Some of this break's ideal conditions are confirmed by sources; others rest on limited evidence. It is the class the app computes from the evidence (how well the break's ideal conditions are documented), not a forecast and not a probability.

Main gaps:

- Sources disagree about the wave size this break works in.
- Limited information is available about the swell period this break needs.
- No survey, scientific or official source confirms the best swell direction.
- No survey, scientific or official source confirms the best wind direction.

| Variable | Research confidence | Evidence |

| Swell direction | Moderate | Supported by 4 independent sources, including a forecast site's spot guide. |
| Swell size | Low | Supported by 2 independent sources, including a surf magazine; 1 disagrees. |

| Wind | Moderate | Supported by 3 independent sources, including a forecast site's spot guide. |

| How the wave breaks | High | Described by 4 independent sources, including an encyclopedia entry. |

Research notes (research_evidence.json):

> Eight readable sources from six publishers (Surf-Forecast, Wikipedia, WSL x3, El Salvador Travel, surftrips.co, Surfsphere). WIND: support for a N to NNE offshore: Surf-Forecast NNE, surftrips N, Surfsphere N/NE. The profile's 20 deg fits. CAUTION: a WSL-hosted 2022 forecast post calls NE a sideshore 'devil wind'. Search summaries of Surfer's 'Surf Spot Mechanics' (403, not readable) reportedly say NW is the best offshore and NE is unfavorable sideshore. If confirmed, the profile's 20 deg may be too far east. TIDE CONFLICT: 'all tides' (Wikipedia, El Salvador Travel, surftrips) against mid-to-high (WSL forecast post) and low-to-mid (Surfsphere). Wikipedia says low gives more barrels; WSL says low runs smaller; surftrips says low exposes the boulders. The profile's 'mid' sits between them, and no source names mid alone. SIZE: El Salvador Travel gives best 4-8 ft, up to 12 ft; surftrips gives 3-12 ft (it says it is cross-checked against Surfline, Stormrider and WannaSurf, so it is not independent). Wikipedia's good-day 6-8 ft Hawaiian (about 12-16 ft faces) is bigger than both. SEASON: surftrips gives April-October (matches the profile). El Salvador Travel says rideable year-round, most epic March-April. PERIOD: only 'clean groundswells prevail' (Surf-Forecast); no numbers. The 2022 WSL post is Surfline-authored forecast copy hosted on worldsurfleague.com. Only its general tide and wind characterisations were recorded, never forecast numbers. Drop it if Surfline-authored text should be excluded entirely.

## Ideal conditions

Directions are compass degrees the swell or wind comes FROM, ranges clockwise. Heights keep the scale each source states (breaking face, Hawaiian, swell or relative to the surfer); the app's sizes are breaking face heights in feet. Sources are numbered as in [Sources](#sources).

### Swell height

| Field | Research value | Status | Sources | App model setting |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Minimum suitable | 3 ft | documented | S6 | `wave_height_min_ft` 3 ft (breaking face) |
| Ideal range | 4–8 ft (not stated (1.5-2.5 m)) [S5] · 6–8 ft (Hawaiian) [S2] | conflicting | S2, S5 | no separate setting; working range 3–12 ft |
| Maximum suitable | 12 ft | documented | S5, S6 | `wave_height_max_ft` 12 ft (breaking face) |

Notes:

- **Minimum suitable**: surftrips.co gives a working size of 3 to 12 ft and says the swell goes flat below 3 ft; the scale is not stated.
  - S6 (surftrips.co): “Working size is 3 to 12 ft. Below 3 ft the swell goes flat. Above 12 ft it tends to close out.”
  - S6 (surftrips.co): “SSW and SW swells from 3ft to double-overhead-plus are the target window, with light northerly offshores essential to keep it clean.”
- **Ideal range**: El Salvador Travel says the wave is at its best from 4 to 8 ft (1.5 to 2.5 m), while Wikipedia says the upper point gives the best waves on a 6 to 8 ft swell on the Hawaiian scale; the scales differ, and no conversion between them is stated by either source.
  - S5 (El Salvador Travel (official tourism site)): “Although it can reach up to 12 feet (4 meters), the wave is at its best from 4 to 8 feet (1.5 to 2.5 meters), with swells coming from the southwest.”
  - S2 (Wikipedia): “On a good day, when the swell is 6 to 8 feet high (Hawaiian scale), the upper part of the point produces the best waves”
- **Maximum suitable**: surftrips.co says it tends to close out above 12 ft and El Salvador Travel says it can reach up to 12 ft (4 m); scales are not stated.
  - S6 (surftrips.co): “Working size is 3 to 12 ft. Below 3 ft the swell goes flat. Above 12 ft it tends to close out.”
  - S5 (El Salvador Travel (official tourism site)): “Although it can reach up to 12 feet (4 meters), the wave is at its best from 4 to 8 feet (1.5 to 2.5 meters), with swells coming from the southwest.”

## Conflicting information

- **Swell height · ideal range**: El Salvador Travel says the wave is at its best from 4 to 8 ft (1.5 to 2.5 m), while Wikipedia says the upper point gives the best waves on a 6 to 8 ft swell on the Hawaiian scale; the scales differ, and no conversion between them is stated by either source.
- **Tide · preferred stage**: Wikipedia, El Salvador Travel and surftrips.co say all tides (Wikipedia: low tide probably gives more barrels; surftrips.co: low tide exposes the boulders and makes sections shallower), while Surfsphere gives low and mid tide as best.
- **Seasonality · prime months**: surftrips.co says it fires from April through October, while El Salvador Travel advises a trip from March to April for the powerful south Pacific storm swells.
